title_original: Portraits of Independence: Sanlé Sory Captures a Nation in Colour
excerpt_original: At the Photographers’ Gallery in London, UK, Sanlé Sory: Colour Years reveals a lesser-known chapter in the Burkinabé photographer’s career, documenting changing identities, cultural expression and everyday life in post-independence Burkina Faso. 17 November 2026 […]

blocks.text: At the Photographers’ Gallery in London, UK, Sanlé Sory: Colour Years reveals a lesser-known chapter in the Burkinabé photographer’s career, documenting changing identities, cultural expression and everyday life in post-independence Burkina Faso.

What can a portrait reveal about a society in transformation? In Sanlé Sory: Colour Years, The Photographers’ Gallery revisits the remarkable career of one of West Africa’s most prolific photographers, revealing how colour photography captured the evolving identities and aspirations of a generation. Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.caption: Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.text: Best known for his black-and-white portraits of Bobo-Dioulasso’s vibrant youth culture, Sanlé Sory began experimenting with colour photography in the mid-1980s at his Volta Photo studio. The exhibition presents meticulously restored colour prints from his archive, alongside record covers featuring Volta Jazz, a band associated with Burkina Faso’s flourishing post-independence music scene. From families and couples to traders and shopkeepers, Sory’s portraits document changing fashions, relationships, and everyday experiences in a society negotiating political transformation and cultural exchange.

Established in 1960, the year of Upper Volta’s independence, Volta Photo became a space where individuals could construct and express their identities in front of the camera. Curated by Taous Dahmani, Colour Years offers a perspective on Sory’s enduring photographic legacy, foregrounding the relationship between portraiture, self-representation and social change.

Through colour, fashion and personal expression, the exhibition celebrates the individuals who shaped the visual history of modern Burkina Faso. Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.caption: Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.text: Suzette Bell-Roberts: Sory’s international reputation rests largely on his earlier black-and- white photographs. What drew you to approach his work through colour? What guided your initial research?

Taous Dahmani: I’ve long admired Sanlé Sory’s work, and West African studio photography has interested me for years. Like most people, I knew him through his celebrated black- and-white portraits. But this project began quite simply, with a handful of prints. David Hill, one of Sory’s gallerists, showed me some colour portraits Sory made from the late 1980s onward, and I was immediately struck by how different they felt.

Then came the archive. Florent Mazzoleni, who keeps Sory’s archive, generously gave me unrestricted access. I opened box after box of colour negatives: thousands upon thousands of portraits, a remarkable body of work that had remained largely unseen. They radiate an energy quite unlike the black-and-white photographs. Being able to immerse myself like that, looking slowly and selecting carefully, is what shaped Sanlé Sory: Colour Years . Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.caption: Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.text: What did the colour negatives reveal about the development of Sory’s photographic language, especially in relation to the work for which he is best known?

First, it’s worth remembering how close we came to losing these negatives. Sanlé Sory made well over a million photographs in his career. But in the late 2000s, convinced that no one would ever be interested in his pictures again, he began burning parts of his archive. The colour negatives we have today survived because his archive keeper had the foresight to rescue and preserve several thousand.

Above all, they reveal a photographer who never stood still. Sory trained in black and white, and that is the work he is best known for. But as colour became increasingly popular in the mid-1980s, he embraced it, working mainly with Konica 35mm film alongside Kodak and Agfa. His clients wanted more contemporary forms of self-representation, and he adapted. By the late 1980s, colour was central to his practice.

Rather than repeating the formulas that had served him so well, he kept renewing his approach in response to new technologies, changing fashions and the aspirations of the people in front of his camera. That restlessness comes from a deep fascination with photography itself. Sory was never interested only in taking pictures or in the finished image. He was captivated by every part of the process, from cameras and film to developing and printing. He is a true craftsman who knows every stage of the medium.

I wanted the exhibition to offer a representative cross-section of that practice, from identity photographs to studio portraits. One of its real discoveries is his photographs of market vendors. They take his portraiture out of the studio and into the everyday life of his community, adding a whole new dimension to his work. Fittingly, Sory still goes to the market every day.

Then there are the self-portraits. Throughout his career, Sory kept stepping in front of his own camera to play with identity, performance and self-fashioning. These playful, self-aware images feel strikingly contemporary. So the archive isn’t simply a record of one place and one time. It shows a photographer who stayed curious, inventive and fully engaged with what photography could do, from his first black-and-white portraits to the colour years. Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.caption: Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.text: What do we know about the circumstances under which Sory adopted colour photography, and how did this affect his work, technically and commercially?

Sanlé Sory opened his Volta Photo studio in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960. Over the next six decades, he built an archive estimated at more than a million photographs: an extraordinary record of the changing lives, fashions and aspirations of his community. He trained in black and white and turned to colour in the mid-1980s, as it grew in popularity. When asked why, he gave a wonderful answer: “When you are in a place where everybody dances, you have to try to dance like everybody else!”

On one level, then, the move was practical. As colour photography became more widely available, his clients asked for it, and Sory adapted. But the more time I spent with the negatives, the more I saw something deeper at work. By asking for colour, his sitters asked Sory to keep pace with technology and with a new generation eager to belong to a contemporary vision of Burkina Faso and West Africa, beyond colonial framings. Colour let them stake their claim to the present and to a global contemporary moment. It freed them from the nostalgia that black and white so easily invites, and from fantasies of some bygone past. This was also a period of major social and political transformation in Burkina Faso, and colour arrived with a renewed sense of modernity and possibility. Sory’s studio became a place where people could have portraits made that captured far more than their clothes and their poses. In these photographs you glimpse a generation living through a society in transition, with all its hopes and uncertainties. To me, they are images of self-determination and self-representation, carrying new confidence and momentum in West African modernity.

That is what the exhibition sets out to show. Something as seemingly simple as adopting colour opens onto another history, rooted in local aspirations and lived experience rather than framed through a European lens. Photography gave people greater control over how they were seen, beyond colonial and postcolonial expectations, and I wanted the exhibition to make room for that history. Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.caption: Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.text: Looking closely at the portraits themselves, what distinctions emerge in the relationship between Sory, his sitters and the images they made together?

Sory worked through several decades of profound political and social change in Burkina Faso. What can his photographs tell us about changing circumstances in Bobo-Dioulasso, and where do the limits of photographic evidence become apparent? These photographs span a period of enormous political, social, and cultural change in Burkina Faso, from the final years of Thomas Sankara’s revolution through the decades that followed. Sory’s studio quietly recorded these transformations, not through grand historical events but through ordinary people choosing how to present themselves.

The colour photographs let us see history in a very different way. Black-and- white images have rightly become iconic, but they can also create a sense of distance and timelessness. Colour brings us much closer to the lived reality of the period. Suddenly you notice the fashions, the fabrics, the painted backdrops, the arrival of global brands, the changing aspirations of a new generation and the confidence with which people fashioned their own identities. For me, colour is not simply a technical or aesthetic shift; it marks a new chapter in Burkina Faso’s modern history. It reflects a society looking forward rather than being defined by its colonial past. These portraits are acts of self-representation, allowing Burkinabè people to define themselves on their own terms. Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.caption: Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.text: The exhibition includes studio portraits, photographs of traders and record covers. What informed your selection and arrangement of these materials, and what connections emerged during the curatorial process?

I wanted the exhibition to move the way Sory himself moved: out of the studio and into the city. Three bodies of work emerged from the archive, and together they show how one photographer captured a whole community’s way of seeing itself. The record covers had to be there. Sory was commissioned to photograph the sleeves for Volta Jazz, and they are among his earliest colour works. As he recalled in conversation: “He [Idrissa Koné] had paid for colour film, so we went to Bobo’s municipal garden and across town. All Volta Jazz members wore red suits, with a yellow tuxedo reserved for the conductor. Volta Jazz created the soundtrack for Bobo’s joyful parties and daily happiness. Mixing Afro-Cuban rhythms, Congolese rumba and Mandingo traditions with lyrics in Dioula, Volta Jazz created a sound all its own. They played the landmark Pan-African Cultural Festival in Algiers in 1969 and toured regularly in Côte d’Ivoire. More than a band, they became a cultural institution and a symbol for young people, capturing the optimism of the post-independence years.

The market photographs were the great discovery. They had never been shown, never studied, never even considered. From the late 1980s to the 2010s, Sory took his camera into Bobo-Dioulasso’s central market. Burkina Faso’s second-largest city has long been a crossroads of trade, movement and cultural exchange, and its market is where commerce, work and social life meet. Sory photographed the traders, artisans and shopkeepers who kept it running, showing vendors alongside the goods they sold. It was good business too: the market helped him expand his clientele. What connects everything is performance. In the studio, at the market, or in a park with a band in red suits, Sory’s subjects always show us who they are, or who they want to be. The market portraits continue the approach of his studio work, but now the stage is public. Seen together, they reveal a photographer who understood that a portrait is a collaboration, and a city that knew exactly how it wanted to be seen. Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.caption: Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.text: Sory’s work has entered international photographic history largely through a particular period and visual vocabulary. What does his reception reveal about how African photographic practices have been researched, collected and historicised?

Sory’s reception follows a familiar pattern. Like several of his West African contemporaries, he entered international photographic history through his black-and- white studio portraits from the 1960s to the early 1980s. The story told about that work has often centred on a single moment: the elegant, optimistic years after independence. Those images are extraordinary, but treating them as the whole story risks freezing African photography in a nostalgic past, as if its modernity stopped when the film changed.

I see Sory’s black-and-white portraits as belonging to the first postcolonial articulation of modernity in Burkina Faso. Independence came in 1960, but as Frederick Cooper has argued, sovereignty changed hands faster than institutions, economies, or political imaginaries. In Upper Volta, as the country was then known, independence aspirations unfolded within frameworks still deeply marked by colonial development models and continued French influence. Sory’s sitters present themselves as confident, elegant and cosmopolitan. Modernity appears as a performance: an aspiration enacted before the camera.

Sory’s photographs show how everyday photographic practice absorbed broader shifts in the political imagination. If the black-and-white archive records a generation performing modern life within inherited colonial frameworks, the colour years belong to a moment when modernity itself was being redefined: no longer a condition inherited from colonialism, but a project authored from within Africa. That is what a narrow reception misses. Colour here is more than a technical process. It embodies the right to determine how Burkina Faso should be seen, through its own lens. Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.caption: Sanlé Sory. Volta Photo Studio, Bobo-Dioulasso, Burkina Faso. © Sanlé Sory, 2026. Courtesy of Tezeta.

blocks.text: In preparing Colour Years , which aspects of Sory’s archive proved most difficult to interpret, and what questions about his practice remain unresolved?

The hardest thing to read wasn’t the photography itself but everything the sitters brought into the frame. Sory’s clients dressed with intent, and in the colour years their clothes carry a dense layer of meaning that I needed help to decode. I’m hugely grateful for the insights of Catherine E. McKinley, the writer and expert on African textiles and photography, which shaped how I read these pictures. Take the pagne, which appears throughout the archive. Across Francophone West Africa, the term refers to a two-yard length of cloth, often wrapped around the waist but also worn as a headwrap, used as a baby carrier or a ceremonial covering, or as a support for carrying loads. How it is worn varies with region, age, marital status and occasion. Pagnes are passed down through generations and tied to birth, marriage and other milestones. Fine wax prints also held real economic value: women bought, traded and carefully preserved them. Their motifs carry social messages, so cloth is as much a form of visual communication as dress.

Naming is part of that language. Not every design has a name, but those that do can become iconic, and names shift across national, ethnic, and regional lines. Wax prints began as a European industrial product. Yet by naming them, African traders, retailers and consumers made them their own, turning colonial commodities into objects with local meaning, value and authorship. Then there’s a newer layer. In the late 1980s and 1990s, political change brought new influences. Hip hop, inspired in part by Kurtis Blow and Grandmaster Flash, shaped fashions and attitudes. Nike and Adidas arrived, often through the second-hand markets known locally as yougou-yougou. Young people didn’t simply adopt these styles. They combined them with local textiles to express both individuality and cultural pride. Much remains unresolved. The portraits circulated as personal keepsakes, not named artworks, so most sitters are unidentified, and we’ve chosen not to impose retrospective titles. Many of the cloth designs they wear may once have had names we can no longer recover. And the surviving colour negatives are only a fraction of what Sory made. They show a generation confidently blending local traditions with global influences, but we still don’t know much about the people in them.
This exhibition is on view at The Photographers’ Gallery in London until 21 February 2027.
